clarent.overview: Excalibur is the mythical sword of King Arthur that was purported to possess magical powers and be associated with the rightful sovereignty of Britain. Its first reliably datable appearance is found in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae. Excalibur as the "sword in the stone" functioning as the proof of Arthur's lineage is an iconic motif featured throughout most works dealing with Arthur's youth since its introduction in Robert de Boron's Merlin. The sword given to the young Arthur by the Lady of the Lake in the tradition that began soon afterwards with the Post-Vulgate Cycle is not the same weapon, but in Thomas Malory’s Le Morte d'Arthur they share the name of Excalibur.

claiomh-solais.overview: The Sword of Light or Claidheamh Soluis (Old Irish; modern Irish: Claíomh Solais [ˌklˠiːw ˈsˠɔlˠəʃ]) is a trope object that appears in a number of Irish and Scottish Gaelic folktales. The "Quest for sword of light" formula is catalogued as motif H1337. The sword appears commonly as a quest object in the Irish folktale of a hero seeking "The One Story" (or the "Cause of the one story about women"), which culminates in the discovery of a "Tale of the Werewolf" (a man magically turned wolf by an unfaithful wife). However, the sword is uninvolved in the man-wolf portion, and only figures in the hero-adventure frame story.

dragon.overview: A dragon is a mythical creature found in the folklore of cultures throughout the world. It is roughly serpentine in form, and often possesses features drawn from different animals, such as wings and claws. In nearly all cultures, it is conceived of as a powerful and awe-inspiring creature. Dragon-like creatures appear in ancient Mesopotamian art, where they could be hostile or benevolent. In East Asia, dragons were usually regarded as positive beings; Chinese dragons were thought to govern the rain, the sea, and other forms of water, and from the Han dynasty onwards they were emblems of imperial power.

article.html:
Thor's hammer is a weapon with a homely side. It smashes the skulls of giants, and it also raises a pair of goats from their bones so a poor farmer's family can eat again. It kills a wedding party, and it hallows a wedding. This doubleness (violence in the service of order, force that blesses) is what made the hammer the Norse symbol of protection.

Its making is a comedy of error. A fly stings, a smith pauses, the handle comes out short. The gods do not care: the hammer's power is in its striking face and in the fact that it always comes back. Norse myth often gives its greatest treasures a flaw, as if perfection were not quite the point. What matters is that the hammer works, and that it is on the side of the gods.

The Þrymskviða shows the hammer as the hinge of the cosmos. Without it the gods are helpless; to get it back, the god of thunder must put on a bridal veil and pretend to be the goddess of love. The poem is among the funniest in the Eddas, and also a little frightening: the order of the world depends on a single object, and that object can be stolen.

Archaeology gives the hammer a second life, on the necks of real people. In the tenth century men and women wore tiny hammers of silver and iron, and the mould from Trendgården cast hammers and crosses in the same stone. It is a vivid picture of an age of conversion, when the same smith served two gods and the same household might pray to both.

Today the hammer hangs again on the necks of believers, and its meaning is argued over. For Heathens it is a sacred sign of protection and kinship; for others, a comic-book prop; for a few, wrongly, a banner of hate. The old stories suggest an answer: the hammer belongs to the one who uses it to hold back chaos, not to the giants who steal it.

lifetime.html: Thunder gods with weapons appear across the Indo-European world: Indra's vajra, Zeus's thunderbolt, Perun's axe. Bronze Age rock carvings in Scandinavia show figures holding axes or hammers aloft, which some read as early thunder gods.wp

In the tenth century, small hammer pendants of silver, iron and amber were worn across Scandinavia and the Viking world, over a thousand of them now known. A soapstone mould from Trendgården in Denmark could cast hammers and Christian crosses side by side, a craftsman serving both faiths. Runestones such as the Glavendrup stone ask Thor to hallow the runes. The myths themselves were written down by Christian Icelanders in the thirteenth century: the Poetic Edda and Snorri's Prose Edda.wp
Icelandic magical staves and folk belief kept some of the old figures alive, while scholars from the seventeenth century began to publish and translate the Eddas.wp

Nineteenth-century Romantic nationalism made Thor a national hero in art and poetry. In the twentieth century the hammer became the emblem of Heathenry (Ásatrú), reborn in Iceland in 1972, and of popular culture, from Marvel's comic-book Thor (from 1962) to heavy metal. In 2013 the US Department of Veterans Affairs added "Thor's Hammer" to the emblems of belief allowed on military headstones.wp

myth.html:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (c. 1220) tells how it was made. Loki cut off the golden hair of Sif, Thor's wife, and to save his life promised to have the dwarves make her new hair. He then bet his head that the brothers Brokkr and Eitri (Sindri in some versions) could not make treasures as good as those of the sons of Ivaldi. As Eitri worked the forge, a fly (Loki in disguise) stung Brokkr to make him stop pumping the bellows; at the last moment it drew blood from his eyelid, he paused, and the hammer came out with a handle a little too short. Even so the gods judged it the best of all the treasures, for it would protect them against the giants.prose

Thor wields it with two other treasures: the iron gloves Járngreipr and the belt of strength Megingjörð. In the Eddic poem Þrymskviða, the giant Thrym steals the hammer and will return it only if Freyja marries him. Thor goes in her place, dressed as the bride; when the giants lay the hammer in the bride's lap to hallow the wedding, he seizes it and kills them all.poeticprose

The hammer also blesses and restores. Thor hallows the funeral pyre of Baldr with it, and he kills his goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr for supper, then raises them from their bones with Mjölnir the next morning. At Ragnarök, after Thor dies fighting the Midgard Serpent, his sons Móði and Magni inherit the hammer.prosepoetic

The Christian writers who preserved the myths treat Thor with humour and affection: his strength, his temper, his comic disguise as Freyja. The hammer is the guarantee that the gods' world holds against chaos.prosepoetic
